description: We are two enthusiastic high school students with a shared passion for science, technology, and innovation. Driven by our curiosity about space exploration and emerging technologies, we are eager to apply our technical knowledge and creative thinking to real-world challenges.
summary: OXV is a toolkit for understanding fire in microgravity, made of two tools: the OXV Simulator and the OXV Research Workstation. The Simulator is a real-time 3D flame model written in C++ and OpenGL. Users control gravity, fuel, oxygen, pressure, inert gas and airflow, and watch the flame respond. Presets recreate NASA scenarios such as a lunar-habitat atmosphere, a FLEX droplet and Apollo’s pure-oxygen cabin. Its physics reproduces trends NASA observed in flight: spherical flames, radiative extinction and FLEX’s invisible “cool flames”. The Research Workstation is a dashboard that makes 16 NASA PSI investigations usable. It classifies and ranks studies, tracks DOIs and dataset versions, and charts 274 FLEX flight runs to show where flames survive or go out. A local AI assistant answers questions and checks every citation before showing it. Fire in a spacecraft behaves nothing like fire on Earth, and that gap has cost lives, from Apollo 1 to the Mir fire. The Simulator shows what a space fire looks like; the Workstation shows what NASA measured, so designers, researchers and students can see a scenario and look up the evidence behind it.
details:
The OXV Simulator is a real-time 3D fire model. Users set gravity (0–2 g, with tilt and jitter), choose one of eight fuels, and adjust oxygen level, pressure, temperature and the inert gas (N₂, CO₂ or helium). They can also add wind or cabin ventilation and switch between a burner and a free-floating droplet. Each time-step runs seven stages on a 3D grid: boundaries, advection, buoyancy, diffusion, ignition, combustion and a pressure solve. A GPU volume renderer then draws the flame. The model includes the effects that make space fires different:

  • Burning is limited by how fast fuel and oxygen mix, which gives flames a physical length.
  • Large flames lose heat by radiation and can go out.
  • Droplets can keep reacting as invisible “cool flames” after the visible flame disappears, as NASA’s FLEX experiments found.

Presets recreate NASA scenarios: a lunar-habitat atmosphere (70.3 kPa, 30% O₂), a CO₂-suppressed FLEX droplet, burning PMMA on the ISS, and an Apollo-style pure-oxygen cabin. While the simulation runs, the user sees live readouts, graphs, a fire-risk index and a local AI assistant that answers questions about the current run. A validation suite checks every preset against known trends. All 12 pass.

The OXV Research Workstation is a dashboard over 16 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations. A pipeline cleans the records, checks their DOIs and keeps every dataset version. Three explainable models then work on the catalogue:

  • A topic classifier, which shows the words behind each label it assigns.
  • A hybrid ranker, which shows how it weighted meaning, keywords, metadata and evidence quality.
  • A research assistant, which checks every citation against the evidence it retrieved and removes any it cannot verify.

The Workstation has seven views: overview, explorer, ranking, comparison, assistant, provenance and telemetry. The telemetry view reads raw flight tables, including 274 FLEX droplet runs and 129 BASS-II tests.

Benefits

  • Mission designers can see how a proposed cabin atmosphere changes fire behaviour before building anything.
  • Researchers can find the right NASA experiment, with its dataset version and DOI, in seconds instead of searching scattered archives.
  • Students and the public can see why a space flame becomes a slow blue sphere.
  • Everyone can see the Workstation’s reasoning: ranking weights are shown, labels come with their evidence, and the assistant won’t present an answer it can’t back with a source.

Intended impact

Fire in a spacecraft behaves nothing like fire on Earth, and that gap has cost lives: Apollo 1 in 1967 and the Mir fire in 1997. NASA has more than three decades of microgravity combustion data, but it is fragmented and difficult to use. OXV aims to make that knowledge easy to see and to search, to support safer habitat design for Artemis and beyond, and to feed back into fire safety and cleaner combustion on Earth.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Simulator: C++17, OpenMP (multithreaded solver), OpenGL 3.3 (volume rendering), Dear ImGui and GLFW (interface), CMake.
  • Workstation: Python 3.11, Streamlit, Pydantic v2, scikit-learn with a pure-Python fallback, matplotlib, and a fallback server built only on the Python standard library.
  • AI: Ollama running the qwen3.5:4b model locally. No cloud services and no API keys.
  • Data: NASA PSI repository (FLEX / PSI-69, BASS-II and others), plus NASA incident histories.
  • Hardware: one desktop PC with an Intel i5-12400F, 32 GB RAM, an RTX 3050 (6 GB) and Ubuntu.
  • Quality checks: a C++ validation suite for the physics and 26 Python unit tests.

Creativity

Most fire tools offer either a visualisation or a database. OXV puts both side by side: see what a fire does, then check what NASA measured in comparable experiments. The simulator treats unsteadiness as physics rather than decoration, so microgravity flames sit eerily still while 1 g flames flicker, as in real footage. It also models the cool-flame hazard, where a fire looks extinguished but is not. On the research side, the assistant is built to refuse rather than invent a source, which matters when the topic is crew safety.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy versus speed: a full combustion simulation can’t run in real time on a single PC, so we chose models that reproduce NASA-observed trends at interactive speed. We say plainly that this is a trend model, not certified CFD.
  • Trust: every answer traces back to a DOI and a dataset version, and ranking and classification decisions are explainable.
  • Offline use: everything runs locally, with no internet, accounts or paid services.
  • Limits we know about: the coarse grid shortens 1 g flames, and the catalogue is small, which holds the classifier’s score down (macro-F1 0.48). Our next steps target both: calibrating against PSI flight data and expanding to more than 300 NASA records.
  • Accessibility: the interface works for an expert tuning pressure or a student moving one gravity slider.
